messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: simplifying auto-dif special functions
parts:
I think I've figured out how to make writing special
functions for doubles, forward-mode auto-dif and
reverse-mode auto-dif much much simpler.

Let me start with what it looks like from the perspective
of someone writing a new unary special function. I'll use exp()
as an example. First, there's a static support struct
that defines two functions:

struct exp_fun {
static inline double f(double x) {
return std::exp(x); // f(x) = exp(x)
}
static inline double df(double /*x*/, double fx) {
return fx; // d/dx f(x) = exp(x) = f(x)
}
};

Then we need to write the actual function, which I call my_exp()
here to avoid name conflicts:

template <typename T>
inline T my_exp(const T& x) {
return apply<exp_fun>(x);
}

That's it. Now it'll work with doubles, forward-mode, and reverse-mode
auto-diff.

Here's what we need for support for doubles:

template <class F>
inline double apply(double x) {
return F::f(x);
}

Here's what we need for support for forward-mode auto-dif:

template <class F, typename T>
inline fvar<T> apply(const fvar<T>& x) {
T fx = F:f(x.val_);
return fvar<T>(fx, x.d_ * F::df(x.val_, fx)); // chain rule
}

For reverse mode, we need a function and a support class:

template <class F>
inline var apply(const var& x) {
return var(new fun_vari<F>(x));
}

where the fun_vari class is defined as:

template <class F>
struct fun_vari : public op_v_vari {
fun_vari(var x)
: op_v_vari(F::f(x.vi_->val_), x.vi_) {
}
virtual void chain() {
avi_->adj_ += adj_ * F::df(avi_->val_,val_); // chain rule
}
};

I haven't tested forward mode, but reverse works like a charm.
There shouldn't be any runtime overhead for any of this, either,
compared to how we're doing things now. It'll let us get rid
of roughly a gazillion vari implementation classes with highly redundant
code.

It'd also be easy to extend this framework to map unary functions. Mapping
combined with how we vectorized the matrix and prob functions led me
down this route. The savings are going to be even greater in terms
of effort for binary and ternary functions and their mixed vectorization,
which are pretty much impossible to do any other way.

- Bob
